newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Premier could be sacked soon -Interfax.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Premier could be sacked soon -Interfax.

text.p: A Ukrainian news agency reported on Thursday that Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko might soon be sacked, but aides to the premier said his political life was not in danger.
President Leonid Kuchma could issue a decree sacking Lazarenko soon, Interfax-Ukraine news agency quoted informed sources in the capital as saying on Thursday.
"The agency will have to make a correction. He will survive. There are no grounds to expect this decree," one top aide told Reuters on hearing of the report.
Interfax quoted an "informed source" as saying there was a "very high probability that the decree will be published in the next few hours".
Lazarenko failed to appear at the evening session of parliament, when deputies were considering this year's long-delayed budget and speaker Olexander Moroz said he was ill.
All the other members of the cabinet were in place, including First Deputy Prime Minister Vasyl Durdynets.
But a spokesman for the presidential administration could not confirm any such decree existed, saying by telephone: "At this moment, 3.15 p.m. (1215 GMT), there is no decree".
Another Lazarenko aide said his team had heard earlier that moves were afoot to remove him, but added: "As far as I recall this is at least the third time there have been such rumours".
Western officials are said to have been pushing for Lazarenko's dismissal amid allegations of high-level government corruption and failure to make the reform process effective.
The 44-year-old former regional leader is a member of the so-called "Dnipropetrovsk Clan" of powerful figures from the eastern industrial heartland of the former Soviet republic of 51 million people.
Kuchma once headed the Soviet Union's biggest missile plant in the city while Lazarenko occupied top posts in the regional administration.

But Ukraine, third in line for U.S. aid after Israel and Egypt, is under mounting pressure from Western partners to reform, and the government and parliament have been accused of lacking the will to attack corruption.
The prime minister's position has weakened since last week as the pro-Kuchma People's Democratic Party and several groups in parliament have called on the president to sack him.

Kuchma himself has repeatedly criticised the prime minister and his government for failing to push this year's budget and tax reforms underpinning it through parliament, but Lazarenko has so far escaped a months-long cabinet reshuffle.

Lazarenko met striking miners on Wednesday and warned that if he were sacked -- a step which would force Kuchma to re-appoint the cabinet -- workers would wait at least another six months for a mountain of unpaid wages.
If Lazarenko were sacked, he would be the fifth prime minister to be dismissed in post-Soviet Ukraine.
His predecessor Yevhen Marchuk was sacked in May 1996 and accused of mishandling the economy and promoting his own political image.
